newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG army remains on alert to protect Singirok.
newsitem.headline: PNG army remains on alert to protect Singirok.

text.p: Heavily-armed soldiers guarded Papua New Guinea's main army headquarters Murray Barracks on Monday despite police saying there were no orders to arrest sacked army boss Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok.
Singirok, who led an army revolt in March which forced prime minister Sir Julius Chan to step aside, lives inside Murray Barracks and is still in effective control of the army.

Police met soldiers in Murray Barracks on Monday to allay fears that Singirok was to be arrested, but despite the reassurances armed soldiers remained on guard behind sandbags at the gates to Murray Barracks.
"That was misinformation, there were no orders for Singirok's arrest," police operations commander Ludwig Campbell told Reuters.
"The police will not arrest anyone in the defence force unless it has informed the department of defence and office of the commander," he said.
Police and army sources earlier said orders had been given for Singirok's arrest. But police did arrest Jonathan Oata, secretary of PNG Watch Council, a human rights organisation.
Oata, who led protests in March, was charged with two counts of unlawful assembly during the anti-Chan protests.

In March, Singirok demanded Chan resign within 48 hours over a plan to hire 70 African mercenaries to help end a secessionist revolt on resource-rich Bougainville island, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.
Singirok said the US$36 million mercenary deal was corrupt.

Chan sacked Singirok, sparking an army revolt which eventually saw Chan step aside pending the outcome of a judicial inquiry into the mercenary deal. Singirok has said the inquiry, which ends on May 30, will be a whitewash. PNG is due to hold national elections from June 14.
